comparison: Both evaluate the VR system validation (C49-C65). OpenEval finds the system SUPPORTED with robust controls and statistical validation. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 2's concerns about 120 FPS frame rate producing 15mm jumps and questioning whether fish perceive continuous motion, though other reviewers found it sophisticated and post-revision the manuscript improved.

Both address reprogramming evidence (C5, C48, C66-C80). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with converging evidence from training data and critical tests. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN - while accepting the reprogramming itself as 'remarkable,' Reviewer 2 challenges the foundational 40ms reaction time claim, arguing it relies on insufficient support and questioning the 'reflex-like' characterization that is central to the paper's framing.

Both evaluate generalization across untrained dimensions (C6, C81-C94). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with statistical evidence of immediate generalization without learning curves. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED - all reviewers accepted these findings, with Reviewer 3 praising the 'impressive' learning and ability to use the rule 'in a variety of novel situations.'

Both assess dual-rule operation (C7, C95-C109). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with evidence of simultaneous shape-based rule selection. Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED - reviewers uniformly accepted this as a 'remarkable finding' demonstrating fish can 'master simultaneously two decision-making rules based on different shape of objects' with no methodological concerns raised.

Both address speed-accuracy tradeoff absence and reflex-speed claims (C8, C79, C110, C120). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with no correlation between error and latency. Peer review rates it UNSUPPORTED - Reviewer 2 explicitly challenges the 40ms claim as having 'little support,' noting previous studies show 60-75ms latencies, and criticizes mentioning 40ms in abstract as 'overselling the result.'

Both evaluate the broader conclusion about challenging speed-flexibility dichotomy (C115, C147). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED as challenging prevailing views. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN - while editor and Reviewer 3 endorsed the broad relevance, Reviewer 2's challenge to the reflex-speed characterization undermines the foundation, questioning whether these truly represent high-speed decisions being contrasted with flexible cognition.

Both address sample size and individual variation concerns (C135-C136). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting authors appropriately acknowledge limitations with reasonable defense. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN - Reviewer 3 explicitly requested individual performance data, stating it's 'essential for appreciating the flexibility of the system,' though post-revision concerns were adequately addressed.

Partial overlap on learning dynamics (C74). OpenEval's R2 includes C74 as part of broader SUPPORTED reprogramming evidence. Peer review R8 rates presentation of learning timeline UNCERTAIN - Reviewer 3 requested clarification on 'how long did this process last' and whether temporal aspects were 'explained in a proper way,' though this was addressed in revision.

OpenEval finds rapid rule selection without prior information (C106-C109) SUPPORTED, showing decisions remain appropriate when shape revealed only at motion onset. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these claims, though they overlap with dual-rule results accepted in peer R4.

OpenEval finds baseline ballistic mapping behavior (C39-C45) SUPPORTED, establishing foundation for reprogramming experiments based on prior work. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these background claims, though they provide context accepted throughout peer review.

OpenEval finds theoretical framework and prevailing view (C1-C3, C9-C12, C21-C25) SUPPORTED by established literature citations. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background/motivation claims, though peer R6 questions whether the study successfully challenges this framework.

OpenEval finds empirical examples of rapid decisions without speed-accuracy tradeoffs (C13-C20) SUPPORTED by peer-reviewed literature. No peer review evaluation addresses these contextual examples from other species, though they provide background for the study's motivation.

OpenEval finds hoverfly interception example (C26-C28) SUPPORTED as canonical inflexible high-speed decision. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses this comparative example, though it serves as contrast to archerfish findings.

OpenEval finds biological context of archerfish hunting (C29-C38) SUPPORTED by multiple citations. No specific peer review evaluation addresses these background claims, though C32 appears in peer R5's evaluation of speed claims.

OpenEval finds authors' initial hypotheses (C46-C47) SUPPORTED as reasonable predictions. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these hypothesis statements, though they provide context for why results are surprising.

OpenEval finds contextual framing about novelty of combination (C116-C122) SUPPORTED, noting individual features aren't novel but combination with speed is unexpected. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses this framing, though it relates to peer concerns about the speed characterization.
OpenEval finds brain size/processing speed analogy (C123-C129) SUPPORTED by insect cognition literature. No peer review evaluation addresses this conceptual framework for interpreting findings.
OpenEval finds neurobiological context about 'functional minibrain' (C130-C133) SUPPORTED by prior work citations. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these mechanistic claims.

OpenEval rates ecological/evolutionary hypotheses (C138-C146) UNCERTAIN, noting speculation is acknowledged but direct evidence for wild prey variation is lacking. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these evolutionary scenarios.
OpenEval finds future research directions (C148-C150) SUPPORTED as appropriately framed open questions. No peer review evaluation addresses these forward-looking statements.

OpenEval finds methodological details (C151-C164) SUPPORTED as clearly stated and internally consistent. No peer review evaluation specifically addresses these methods claims, though peer R1 questions broader VR system adequacy and peer R7 questions sample size.
